justification_text:
My point estimates were anchored primarily to the prevailing price level of the underlying asset at the time of the forecast, with modest directional drift applied at each horizon. For the one-day estimate, I leaned heavily on recent price momentum and mean-reversion tendencies, assuming no major catalysts would materially shift the market within a single session. The one-week estimate incorporated a slight upward bias reflecting the broader trend context, while the one-month estimate extended that drift further, though with diminishing conviction as the compounding uncertainty of a longer horizon makes precise directional calls increasingly speculative. In all three cases, the point estimates represent my best single guess under a relatively benign, trend-continuation scenario.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At the one-day horizon, the narrow band of roughly plus or minus 15 points captures typical intraday-to-next-day volatility, informed by recent realized volatility and the absence of known scheduled events immediately ahead. By one week, the interval widens to about 30 points on each side, accounting for the possibility of earnings surprises, macroeconomic data releases, or shifts in Federal Reserve communication. At one month, the interval expands to roughly 60 to 65 points in either direction, reflecting the much larger space of scenarios that can unfold over four weeks, including changes in sector sentiment, broader index moves, and geopolitical developments that are impossible to predict with precision.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated ranges. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings report, a surprise dovish pivot from the Fed, or a broader market rally driven by risk appetite could easily propel the price above the upper bound of even the one-month interval. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data, a credit event, or a sharp selloff in correlated assets could drive prices below the lower bounds. My intervals are calibrated around normal market conditions, and tail events by definition are underrepresented. A true market shock or liquidity crisis would invalidate the assumptions embedded in all three horizons simultaneously.
